newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico economic policy steady despite poll -Werner.
newsitem.headline: Mexico economic policy steady despite poll -Werner.

text.p: Mexico's economic policy will not be derailed despite heavy losses incurred by the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) in nationwide weekend polls, Deputy Finance Minister Martin Werner said on Monday.

He made the comments in an exclusive interview with Reuters Financial Television, the morning after preliminary results from nationwide elections on Sunday showed the PRI had likely lost its 68-year absolute majority in the lower house of Congress.

"We have lost some ground but the PRI is still the most powerful political party in the country, and we will use our position to push through the right policies," he said in the live television interview -- one of the first by a government official after Sunday's election.
"We will fight for the right program for the Mexican economy," he added.

Preliminary official results showed the PRI had won 38.72 percent of votes for the lower house of Congress against 27.02 percent for the conservative opposition National Action Party (PAN) and 25.65 percent for the left-leaning Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), with 15 percent of the vote still left to count.

Werner said the election outcome would not result in any deviation from current economic policy. "The government will continue to pursue its objectives of sustainable recovery and a less vulnerable economy that doesn't create the imbalances that led to the crisis we had in 1994," he said.
"We will have to do much more consensus building, but given the shared objective of a stronger economy on a sustainable basis, I think there is room for consensus on solid economic growth," he added.

Part of voter rejection of the ruling PRI stemmed from the country's severe 1994-95 recession that has seen a 30 percent decline in real wages. Werner said he expected to see more room available for social spending in the next budget. "We need to increase social spending on a sustainable basis, (which means) you open more room in the budget with solid foundations for stronger revenues," he said.
He pointed to enforcing current fiscal laws and improving admininstration, and lowering interest payments to increase resources.
He said Mexico would clock up 1997 economic growth of at least 4.5 percent.
"Our target for the year is 4.5 percent growth, and it is more likely to be above rather than below target," he said.
